notes.meaning: Paul introduces Phoebe to the believers in Rome, most likely as the trusted messenger carrying this letter. She was a faithful Christian who served the church in Cenchrea, a seaport near Corinth. Paul urges the Roman church to give her a warm reception and honor her dedicated ministry.

differ.view: Wesley and Clarke understand Phoebe as holding an official church role as a deaconess who assisted at women's baptisms and visited the sick.
Some complementarian scholars view Phoebe as holding an official deacon office that was distinct from the male eldership.
Others believe the word servant describes a generous, active helper rather than someone holding an ordained church office.

other.label: Catholic
other.view: Haydock explains that she served in ministry by privately teaching new believers, assisting at female baptisms, and distributing charity.

notes.meaning: Paul asks the Roman Christians to welcome Phoebe as a sister in Christ and to provide any help she might need for her affairs in Rome. She had been a generous patron who used her resources to protect and care for many believers, including Paul. Christians are called to show hospitality and assist those who have spent their lives helping others.

Paul sends warm greetings to Prisca and Aquila, a married couple who labored alongside him in spreading the good news about Jesus. They had risked their own lives to protect Paul from danger. Because of their courage and sacrifice, all the non-Jewish congregations owed them heartfelt gratitude.

Early Christians did not have separate church buildings, so local congregations met in private homes like the one owned by Aquila and Prisca. Paul also greets Epenetus, who was one of the very first people in that region to trust in Christ. Coming to faith early was viewed as a special honor and a sign of a larger spiritual harvest to follow.

Paul greets Mary, a woman who worked tirelessly for the believers in Rome. Even though Scripture gives no other details about her life, her hard work for God's people was noted and remembered with honor.

Paul greets Andronicus and Junia, two Jewish relatives who had shared prison confinement with him for their faith. They had become followers of Christ before Paul did, and he honors their long and faithful walk with the Lord.

differ.view: Many understand the phrase to mean that these two believers were well known to and highly respected by the twelve apostles.
Calvin understood them to be called apostles in a broad sense as traveling missionaries who planted churches.

other.label: Modern scholarship
other.view: Many modern scholars see Junia as a woman who was recognized as an apostle in the broader sense of a traveling missionary.

notes.meaning: Paul greets Ampliatus, describing him as a dearly loved brother in the Lord. This simple greeting shows how faith in Christ creates deep, genuine affection among believers.

Paul sends greetings to Urbanus and Stachys, honoring them as valued helpers and dear friends in Christian work. He also greets Apelles, whose faith had been tested and proven genuine, and the believers living in the household of Aristobulus. Even when the master of a house was not a believer, servants and relatives could belong to Christ.

Paul greets Herodion, a fellow Jewish believer and likely a relative. He also sends greetings to the Christians who worked within the household of Narcissus, showing that God's grace reached into influential Roman estates.

Paul greets Tryphena, Tryphosa, and Persis, three faithful women who devoted themselves to serving the church. Persis is singled out for having worked especially hard in the Lord's work. Their labor proves the vital role women played in spreading the gospel and caring for the church family.
Paul greets Rufus, calling him an outstanding and choice follower of Christ. He also sends love to Rufus's mother, who had cared for Paul so tenderly that he felt she was like a mother to him too.

Paul greets two groups of believers and all the Christians who met together with them, likely in house gatherings. By remembering both named leaders and unnamed saints, Paul shows that every single member of God's family is valued and loved.

Believers are told to greet each other with a holy kiss, which was a common custom showing pure Christian love and family peace. Paul also sends greetings to Rome from all the local churches where he had been serving.

Paul urges the Roman believers to stay on guard against anyone who causes divisions or leads others into sin by teaching things contrary to the truth. Christian unity must be built on sound teaching from the apostles. Believers should avoid close fellowship with those who disrupt the peace of the church.

False teachers may pretend to serve the Lord, but they are really driven by selfish ambition and bodily appetites. They use smooth, flattering words to trick innocent and unsuspecting people. Christians need discernment so they are not misled by pleasing speech.

Paul is glad because the Roman Christians were well known for their willingness to obey God's word. Even so, he wants them to be sharp and wise about what is good, while staying innocent and free from evil schemes. True obedience requires both a willing heart and careful discernment.

Paul promises that God, who gives true peace, will soon crush Satan completely, fulfilling the ancient promise that the serpent's head would be bruised. Even though God wins the battle through Christ, He allows His people to share in the final victory. Paul then prays that the grace of Jesus will strengthen and guide them.

differ.view: Some view this crushing as pointing primarily to the final defeat of Satan at the end of time.
Calvin taught that this promise offered immediate victory over Satan's attacks in their daily struggles, as well as final victory at the last day.

notes.meaning: Paul sends greetings from Timothy, his close partner in ministry, along with other Jewish companions who were with him in Corinth. These greetings helped build strong bonds of fellowship between distant churches.

Tertius, the secretary who wrote down the letter as Paul spoke, adds his own warm greeting to the believers in Rome. His note shows that humble, quiet service behind the scenes is deeply valued in the work of God.

Gaius sends greetings as a generous host who welcomed Paul and provided a meeting place for the entire local church. Erastus, the city treasurer of Corinth, and Quartus, a Christian brother, also send their greetings, showing that the gospel reached both high civic officials and ordinary believers.

Paul repeats his blessing, praying that the grace of the Lord Jesus Christ—His unearned favor and spiritual strength—would be with every believer. This prayer reminds Christians that they depend entirely on God's mercy from start to finish.

other.label: Modern scholarship
other.view: Most early Greek manuscripts omit this verse here, indicating that it was likely copied by later scribes from verse 20 as a traditional ending.

notes.meaning: Paul concludes his letter with high praise to God, who is able to establish and strengthen believers through the gospel of Jesus Christ. God's plan of salvation was hidden in Old Testament shadows for ages, but it is now made plain to all nations so they can trust and obey Him. All glory belongs forever to the only wise God through Jesus Christ.

other.label: Modern scholarship
other.view: Some ancient manuscripts place this closing song of praise at the end of chapter 14 or chapter 15, though scholars agree it forms an authentic part of Romans.
